title: Kettle on Overpass: Tuition Hike Protest Confrontation
premise: A peaceful student-led demonstration against university tuition hikes in a mid-sized college town escalates when a splinter group attempts to block a state highway, prompting riot police to deploy tear gas and kettle hundreds of demonstrators on a pedestrian overpass.

side_A.role: a researcher at a human-rights NGO
side_A.goal: documenting possible excessive force by police against protesters

side_B.goal: preparing criminal charges against protesters for rioting and property damage

documents:
=== DOCUMENT 1: Millbrook Police Department Incident Log — Route 9 Demonstration Response ===

INCIDENT NUMBER: 2023-1114-R09
DATE: November 14, 2023
CLASSIFICATION: Public Demonstration / Crowd Control
PREPARING OFFICER: Sgt. L. Morales, Records Division

1535 — Chief Inspector Raymond Holt issued a verbal dispersal order via LongRanger 3000 acoustic device mounted on Vehicle 14. Order repeated in English and Spanish, three cycles each, over four minutes. Device confirmed audible up to 200 meters from the vehicle per manufacturer specifications and field testing conducted October 2023.

1540 — Sgt. Marcus Vance, riot squad field commander, reported via radio that projectiles were being thrown from the pedestrian overpass toward police lines. Lt. Karen Sadowski, police logistics coordinator, confirmed both stairwell exits at north and south ends of the overpass remained accessible.

1548 — Riot squad deployed CS tear gas canisters. Total of 24 canisters fired over approximately six minutes. Fourteen canisters logged within 30-meter radius of the pedestrian overpass.

1552 — Approximately 40 riot officers formed lines at both ends of the overpass. Lines maintained for 47 minutes.

WEATHER DATA: Millbrook Regional Weather Station (2.1 miles from overpass) recorded wind speeds at 1548 as 4 mph from the northwest.

DEPLOYMENT SUMMARY: 85 officers deployed from Precincts 1, 3, and 6. Of these, 52 were equipped in riot gear.

STRUCTURE NOTE: Pedestrian overpass spanning Route 9 — 4.2 meters wide, 38 meters long, enclosed by 1.4-meter-high concrete barriers on both sides. No exit ramps.

ARREST LOG: Seven individuals arrested for disorderly conduct and obstructing a highway. All released on own recognizance by November 16, 2023.

OFFICER INJURIES: Three officers treated at Millbrook General Hospital Emergency Department between 1615 and 1830 for contusions (two officers) and fractured wrist (one officer).

CIVILIAN CASUALTIES: 23 individuals admitted to Millbrook General Hospital for tear gas exposure treatment between 1630 and 2000, including two with corneal abrasions.

RESIDENTIAL COMPLAINTS: 12 noise and air quality complaints filed by Maple Court Apartments residents between 1600 and 1900. Maple Court Apartments located 85 meters east of overpass, approximately 120 residents.

VIDEO EVIDENCE: Footage from three smartphones and one traffic camera (Route 9 Cam 04) recorded tear gas deployment. Footage shows canisters landing on overpass within 5 meters of demonstrators who had sat down with arms linked.

=== DOCUMENT 2: Witness statement of Dr. Elena Marchetti, Field Researcher, Citizens Rights Watch ===

STATEMENT TAKEN: November 15, 2023, 10:15 AM
LOCATION: Citizens Rights Watch Field Office, 218 College Avenue, Millbrook
STATEMENT TAKEN BY: Det. R. Pham, Internal Affairs Division, Millbrook Police Department

My name is Dr. Elena Marchetti. I am a field researcher employed by Citizens Rights Watch, a non-governmental organization that monitors protest activity and police conduct. I was present at the November 14 demonstration at Millbrook State University in an official observation capacity, wearing a high-visibility vest marked "LEGAL OBSERVER."

I was positioned on the grass embankment approximately 40 meters west of the Route 9 pedestrian overpass. I had been monitoring the demonstration since approximately 1:30 PM, when I arrived at the main quad where approximately 600 demonstrators had gathered for a rally against proposed tuition increases. At 2:45 PM, I observed a group of roughly 80 protesters split from the main rally and begin marching south on College Avenue toward Route 9. I followed at a distance. By 3:20 PM, approximately 50 protesters had positioned themselves across both northbound lanes of Route 9, and traffic was halted. I could see backup extending at least a mile in each direction; I later learned it was 1.2 miles.

At 3:35 PM, I heard Chief Inspector Holt's dispersal order broadcast through the LongRanger 3000 device. I noted the time on my watch. The order was repeated in English and Spanish three times. I timed the full sequence at four minutes. The audio was clearly audible at my position and would have been audible at substantially greater distances — up to 200 meters, I would estimate, based on the volume.

The first tear gas canister was fired only 30 seconds after the dispersal order began, giving demonstrators on the overpass no realistic opportunity to comply before chemical weapons were used against them. I heard the canister discharge before the second repetition of the Spanish-language order had concluded. There was no meaningful interval between the warning and the use of force.

Regarding the overpass itself, I want to note that Prof. Daniel Okafor, an architectural engineer consulted by our organization, visited the site on November 15 and documented that the northern stairwell exit of the overpass was blocked by a parked police van at 3:40 PM, meaning demonstrators had only one viable exit on the south side, effectively trapping them before gas was deployed. I cannot personally confirm the van's position at 3:40 PM because I had relocated by that time, but Professor Okafor's findings are consistent with what I observed of the overall police posture.

I was not on the overpass itself, so I cannot speak to whether projectiles were thrown from it. I will say that from my vantage point, I did not see any objects arcing through the air before the gas deployment, though my line of sight to the far end of the overpass was partially obstructed.

STATEMENT CONCLUDED.
[Signature: Elena Marchetti]

---

=== DOCUMENT 3: Witness statement of Sgt. Marcus Vance, Riot Squad Field Commander, Millbrook Police Department ===

STATEMENT TAKEN: November 15, 2023, 2:00 PM
LOCATION: Millbrook Police Department, Precinct 1, Interview Room B
STATEMENT TAKEN BY: Det. R. Pham, Internal Affairs Division

I am Sergeant Marcus Vance, badge number 4471, riot squad field commander assigned to the November 14 demonstration response. I was on scene from approximately 1:15 PM.

The operation involved 85 officers deployed from three precincts, with 52 in riot gear. We were monitoring the situation at the university quad where approximately 600 demonstrators had gathered. The organizers had a municipal permit for a rally at the quad valid from 12:00 PM to 5:00 PM, but the permit did not authorize marching on public roadways. When approximately 80 protesters split off at 2:45 PM and began marching south on College Avenue toward Route 9, we mobilized.

By 3:20 PM, approximately 50 protesters had positioned themselves across both northbound lanes of Route 9. Traffic was backed up 1.2 miles in each direction. We also had a concentration of approximately 300 demonstrators on the pedestrian overpass. The overpass is 4.2 meters wide and 38 meters long with 1.4-meter-high concrete barriers on both sides and no exit ramps.

Chief Inspector Holt issued the dispersal order at 3:35 PM via the LongRanger 3000. The order was repeated in English and Spanish three times over four minutes, audible up to 200 meters from the vehicle.

A full 13 minutes elapsed between the initial dispersal order and the first canister deployment, during which time officers observed projectiles being thrown from the overpass toward police lines. The gas was deployed at 3:48 PM. We fired 24 canisters over approximately six minutes. Fourteen landed within a 30-meter radius of the overpass.

At 3:52 PM, approximately 40 riot officers formed lines at both ends of the overpass for 47 minutes. This was a containment measure to prevent the situation from escalating further.

Lt. Karen Sadowski, our logistics coordinator, has confirmed that both stairwell exits at the north and south ends of the overpass remained accessible throughout the entire operation, and demonstrators were free to leave via either staircase at any time.

I am aware that Officer Tyrone Beckwith, stationed at the south end of the overpass, reported that at least four glass bottles were thrown from the overpass toward officers between 3:40 PM and 3:47 PM, one of which struck an officer's shield, directly prompting the decision to deploy CS gas.

Three of our officers were treated at Millbrook General Hospital between 4:15 PM and 6:30 PM — two for contusions and one for a fractured wrist. Seven demonstrators were arrested for disorderly conduct and obstructing a highway, all released on their own recognizance by November 16.

I have been informed that the Millbrook County District Attorney's office filed charges against five individuals for reckless endangerment on November 20.

STATEMENT CONCLUDED.
[Signature: Marcus Vance, Sgt.]

---

=== DOCUMENT 4: Witness statement of Jamie Rourke, Student Demonstrator ===

STATEMENT TAKEN: November 16, 2023, 11:00 AM
LOCATION: Millbrook State University Student Union, Room 204
STATEMENT TAKEN BY: Det. R. Pham, Internal Affairs Division, Millbrook Police Department

My name is Jamie Rourke. I am a junior at Millbrook State University. I was a participant in the November 14 protest against proposed tuition increases.

The rally started at 1:00 PM at the main quad. There were about 600 of us there. The student government had passed a resolution on November 10 endorsing the protest and allocating $2,500 for permits and sound equipment. We had a municipal permit for the rally at the quad, valid from 12:00 PM to 5:00 PM. We knew the permit didn't cover marching on public roadways, but the march was organized spontaneously by people who felt the rally alone wasn't enough.

At 2:45 PM, about 80 of us split off and started marching south on College Avenue toward Route 9. By 3:20 PM, about 50 people had sat down across both northbound lanes of Route 9. I went up to the pedestrian overpass with a larger group. There were approximately 300 of us up there. The overpass is 4.2 meters wide and 38 meters long with concrete barriers on both sides about 1.4 meters high. There are no exit ramps. It's essentially a corridor.

I heard the dispersal order at 3:35 PM coming from the police vehicle. It was the LongRanger 3000 device. They repeated it in English and Spanish three times over four minutes. It was loud — you could hear it from 200 meters away, no question.

No one in the group on the overpass threw anything at police. The demonstrators were seated and chanting peacefully when gas canisters began landing among them without any provocation. We were sitting with arms linked. I personally saw canisters land within 5 meters of people who were seated. I know this was also captured on video — there were at least three smartphones recording and a traffic camera.

At 3:52 PM, riot officers — maybe 40 of them — formed lines at both ends of the overpass. We couldn't leave in either direction for 47 minutes. The gas was already in the air. People were choking, crying, vomiting. Some people were screaming. The barriers on the sides are 1.4 meters high — you can't climb over them, and there's a highway below.

I know Dr. Marchetti from Citizens Rights Watch has said the first gas canister was fired only 30 seconds after the dispersal order began. That matches my experience. There was no time to leave even if we had wanted to.

I was not arrested, but I know seven people were arrested for disorderly conduct and obstructing a highway. They were all released by November 16. I also know the DA filed charges against five people for reckless endangerment on November 20.

23 people were admitted to Millbrook General Hospital for tear gas exposure treatment between 4:30 PM and 8:00 PM. Two of them had corneal abrasions.

STATEMENT CONCLUDED.
[Signature: Jamie Rourke]

---

=== DOCUMENT 5: Witness statement of Officer Tyrone Beckwith, Riot Officer, Millbrook Police Department ===

STATEMENT TAKEN: November 16, 2023, 9:30 AM
LOCATION: Millbrook Police Department, Precinct 1, Interview Room B
STATEMENT TAKEN BY: Det. R. Pham, Internal Affairs Division

I am Officer Tyrone Beckwith, badge number 3392. I was assigned to riot squad duty on November 14, 2023, at the Route 9 demonstration response. I was one of 52 officers in riot gear out of a total deployment of 85 officers from three precincts.

I was stationed at the south end of the pedestrian overpass beginning at approximately 3:15 PM. The overpass spans Route 9. It is 4.2 meters wide and 38 meters long, enclosed by 1.4-meter-high concrete barriers on both sides with no exit ramps. There were approximately 300 demonstrators concentrated on the overpass.

At 3:35 PM, Chief Inspector Raymond Holt issued a verbal dispersal order through the LongRanger 3000 acoustic device mounted on a police vehicle. The order was repeated in English and Spanish three times over four minutes. It was audible up to 200 meters from the vehicle.

At least four glass bottles were thrown from the overpass toward officers between 3:40 PM and 3:47 PM, one of which struck an officer's shield, directly prompting the decision to deploy CS gas. I personally witnessed two of the bottles being thrown from the overpass and saw the aftermath of the other two, including the one that hit the shield. The officers behind me can corroborate this.

CS gas was deployed at 3:48 PM. Twenty-four canisters were fired over approximately six minutes. Fourteen landed within a 30-meter radius of the overpass. Wind speeds at that time were 4 mph from the northwest, per the Millbrook Regional Weather Station 2.1 miles from the overpass.

At 3:52 PM, approximately 40 riot officers formed lines at both ends of the overpass, preventing demonstrators from leaving in either direction for 47 minutes. This was standard containment procedure.

I am aware that Sgt. Vance has stated that a full 13 minutes elapsed between the initial dispersal order and the first canister deployment. That is consistent with my understanding of the timeline.

Regarding the exits, Lt. Sadowski has confirmed that both stairwell exits at the north and south ends of the overpass remained accessible throughout the entire operation, and demonstrators were free to leave via either staircase at any time. I was at the south staircase and no one was preventing anyone from walking down those stairs.

I am aware that Capt. Philip Drew, our incident commander, has stated that air monitoring and officer observations confirmed that all CS gas particulate remained within the Route 9 corridor and the overpass area, with no chemical agents reaching any residential structures. The nearest residential buildings are the Maple Court Apartments, 85 meters to the east, housing approximately 120 residents. I know twelve residents filed noise and air quality complaints with the city between 4:00 PM and 7:00 PM, but I cannot speak to the merits of those complaints.

Three officers were treated at Millbrook General Hospital's emergency department between 4:15 PM and 6:30 PM — two for contusions and one for a fractured wrist. Seven demonstrators were arrested for disorderly conduct and obstructing a highway, all released on their own recognizance by November 16. The DA's office filed charges against five individuals for reckless endangerment on November 20.

STATEMENT CONCLUDED.
[Signature: Tyrone Beckwith, Officer]

---

=== DOCUMENT 6: Witness statement of Maria Hensley, Resident, Maple Court Apartments, Unit 4B ===

STATEMENT TAKEN: November 17, 2023, 3:00 PM
LOCATION: Millbrook City Hall, Complaint Intake Office
STATEMENT TAKEN BY: Det. R. Pham, Internal Affairs Division, Millbrook Police Department

My name is Maria Hensley. I am a resident of Maple Court Apartments, Unit 4B. I have lived there for six years. The Maple Court Apartments are located 85 meters east of the Route 9 pedestrian overpass. There are approximately 120 residents in our building.

On November 14, I was home starting around 2:00 PM. I could hear the protest from my apartment — chanting and noise from the direction of the university. Around 3:30 PM it got much louder. I heard a booming voice repeating something in English and Spanish. I later learned this was the police dispersal order through a LongRanger 3000 device. I could hear it clearly even though I was inside with my windows partially open. The device is apparently audible up to 200 meters away, and we are only 85 meters from the overpass.

At approximately 3:48 PM, I smelled something acrid and chemical. It burned my eyes and throat. CS gas entered at least eight apartments on the west-facing side of the Maple Court building through open windows, causing respiratory distress among residents including a 73-year-old with COPD who required ambulance transport. That 73-year-old is my neighbor, Mr. Fenton, in Unit 4A. I called 911 for him myself. He was transported by ambulance at approximately 4:15 PM.

I closed my windows as soon as I realized what was happening, but the gas had already entered. My eyes were burning and I was coughing for the rest of the evening. I did not seek medical treatment, but I know other residents who considered going to the hospital.

I filed a noise and air quality complaint with the city at approximately 5:30 PM on November 14. I know that at least twelve Maple Court residents filed similar complaints between 4:00 PM and 7:00 PM that day.

I am aware that Capt. Philip Drew, the police incident commander, has stated that air monitoring and officer observations confirmed that all CS gas particulate remained within the Route 9 corridor and the overpass area, with no chemical agents reaching any residential structures. I strongly dispute that. I smelled the gas. I felt it in my eyes and lungs. My neighbor was hospitalized. I do not know what air monitoring they conducted, but it does not match what we experienced in this building.

The wind was coming from the northwest at the time. I know this because I checked my weather app after the incident. The Millbrook Regional Weather Station, which is 2.1 miles from the overpass, recorded wind speeds at 3:48 PM as 4 mph from the northwest. Our building is east of the overpass. The gas would have drifted toward us.

STATEMENT CONCLUDED.
[Signature: Maria Hensley]

---

=== DOCUMENT 7: Millbrook General Hospital Emergency Department — Treatment Log Summary ===

DATE: November 14, 2023
DEPARTMENT: Emergency Medicine
ATTENDING: Dr. Priya Nadkarni

PATIENT INTAKE SUMMARY — PROTEST-RELATED TREATMENTS

CIVILIAN PATIENTS (Tear GAS EXPOSURE):
Total admitted: 23
Treatment window: 1630–2000
Presenting symptoms: Ocular irritation, respiratory distress, skin irritation, nausea
Notable injuries: 2 patients with corneal abrasions (confirmed by fluorescein staining)
Treatment provided: Ocular irrigation, supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators as indicated
Dispositions: 19 discharged same evening, 4 held for observation and discharged by November 15 AM

POLICE OFFICER PATIENTS:
Total admitted: 3
Treatment window: 1615–1830
Injuries: 2 officers with contusions (upper extremity and torso), 1 officer with fractured left wrist (confirmed by X-ray)
Treatment provided: Wound care, immobilization, orthopedic consultation for wrist fracture
Dispositions: 2 discharged same evening, 1 officer with fracture referred to orthopedic specialist for follow-up

ADDITIONAL NOTE: 1 civilian patient transported by EMS from Maple Court Apartments (85 meters east of Route 9 overpass) at approximately 1615, presenting with acute respiratory distress, history of COPD. Admitted, treated with bronchodilators and supplemental oxygen, held overnight, discharged November 15.

[Signature: Dr. Priya Nadkarni, Attending Physician, Emergency Medicine]
